title: GDP
objective: After this level you can explain what GDP measures and what it misses.
summary: GDP adds up the market value of the final goods and services a country produces. Real GDP strips out price changes, and GDP misses unpaid work, pollution, leisure and how income is shared.

cards.headline: Cook dinner at home and GDP ignores it. Buy the same meal, and it counts.
cards.body: Same food, same full stomach. The economy's headline number sees only one of them. What it counts, and what it skips, is this level's story.

cards.headline: Everything a country makes, in one number
cards.body: Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the market value of the final goods and services a country produces in a period, such as a quarter or a year. "Final" matters: flour sold to a baker is an input, and only the bread counts. You can add GDP up three ways: the value added at each stage of production, the spending of final buyers, or the incomes everyone earns making it all.

cards.headline: Real GDP: more stuff, not just pricier stuff
cards.body: Remember Level 61? If a country made exactly the same things this year but prices rose, its GDP in money terms would still grow. That's why economists watch real GDP, which adjusts for price changes. Real growth means the economy actually made more, not that the price tags got bigger.

cards.fact: The first US national accounts came with a warning label.
cards.context: In 1934, economist Simon Kuznets presented them to Congress, and warned that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from national income. GDP leaves out unpaid work like housework and volunteering, and ignores pollution, lost leisure and how income is shared. It measures how much a country produces, not how well its people live.

cards.headline: GDP: measured
learned: GDP is the market value of a country's final goods and services
Only final products count, like the bread and not the flour
Real GDP strips out price changes
It misses unpaid work, pollution, leisure and fairness

options.label: The total amount of money held in a country's banks
The average price of a basket of household goods
The total value of everything a country buys from abroad
options.rationale: GDP counts what a country produces.

options.label: The market value of a country's final goods and services

questions.explanation: GDP is the market value of the final goods and services produced in a country in a period.

questions.prompt: You paint your own house instead of hiring a painter. Why doesn't your work show up in GDP?

options.label: Houses are not goods
options.rationale: A hired painter would count; the issue is that your work is unpaid.

options.label: Painting is only an input
options.rationale: The issue is that nobody paid for the work.

questions.explanation: GDP leaves out unpaid work, like housework and volunteering, because it is hard to measure and value.

questions.prompt: GDP can be added up as the incomes everyone earns making it. From Level 11, which incomes are those?

options.label: Prices, taxes, tariffs and fees
options.rationale: Those aren't what the factors of production earn.

options.label: Deposits, loans, bonds and shares
options.rationale: Those are financial assets, not factor incomes.

options.label: Exports, imports, savings and debt
options.rationale: Those aren't the incomes earned from production.

questions.explanation: Land earns rent, labor wages, capital interest and entrepreneurship profit; summed, those incomes are one way to count GDP.
